text:
Sampled ranking scores can change model ordering relative to full-catalog evaluation. RecSys 2025’s [On the Reliability of Sampling Strategies](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086) distinguishes resolution, fidelity, robustness and predictive power; strong discrimination between models does not establish fidelity to full ranking. Thus, two-candidate margins need empirical validation before serving as actionable diagnostics. A [2024 popularity-bias survey](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11257-024-09406-0) also cautions that computational popularity measures rely on assumptions about user benefit; popularity exposure alone cannot establish preference mismatch.

Recommended framework, inferred from these findings: freeze training-prefix probes and candidate sets; compare pairwise margins, fixed multi-negative ranking and full-catalog unseen-item ranking. Stratify by training-only item frequency and history length. For a small, predefined set of component ablations, measure whether diagnostic changes predict category-level validation HR@10 changes, including direction agreement and effect-size association. Bootstrap paired users within each category, preserving baseline–ablation pairing and equal category weights. Treat training-prefix results as diagnostics, since those interactions influenced fitting; keep the pinned 99-negative validation HR@10 as the selection objective.

Repeated validation selection introduces winner’s-curse bias. [A Flexible Defense Against the Winner’s Curse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.18569) addresses inference after selecting an empirical winner, including dependent candidates. Ordinary paired bootstrap intervals quantify user-sampling uncertainty for fixed comparisons; they do not automatically correct adaptive search or training randomness. Predefine ablations, log every trial and checkpoint comparison, report all effects, and label post-selection intervals exploratory. Keep hidden tests untouched and bound diagnostic computation within the shared GPU budget.
